Another triangle ACD is drawn on the outside of AC, D is located to the upper right of C, and there is a right-angle mark at C, indicating that CD is perpendicular to AC. Reasoning: Take coordinates according to the figure as B=(0,0), A=(1,0), C=(0,1). Then AC=sqrt(2), and the perimeter of triangle ABC is 1+1+sqrt(2)=2+sqrt(2). Let CD=t. Because ACD is right-angled at C, AD=sqrt(t^2+2). The perimeters of the two triangles are equal, so sqrt(2)+t+sqrt(t^2+2)=2+sqrt(2), that is, t+sqrt(t^2+2)=2. Squaring gives t=1/2. The direction perpendicular to AC on the outside is, as shown in the figure, (1,1)/sqrt(2), so let s=t/sqrt(2)=1/(2sqrt(2)), then D=(s,1+s). Starting from A, AB=(-1,0), AD=(s-1,1+s). Also |AD|=sqrt((s-1)^2+(1+s)^2)=3/2. Let θ=angle BAD, then cos θ=(1-s)/(3/2), sin θ=(1+s)/(3/2). Therefore sin(2θ)=2sinθcosθ=2*((1+s)/(3/2))*((1-s)/(3/2))=(8/9)(1-s^2). Since s^2=1/8, sin(2 angle BAD)=(8/9)(7/8)=7/9.

Equal perimeters give \sqrt2+t+\sqrt{t^2+2}=2+\sqrt2, so t+\sqrt{t^2+2}=2 and t=1/2. The outward perpendicular direction to AC shown in the image is (1,1)/\sqrt2, so D=(t/\sqrt2,1+t/\sqrt2). Then use \sin(2\theta)=2\sin\theta\cos\theta to obtain \sin(2\angle BAD)=\frac{8}{9}(1-s^2)=\frac{8}{9}(1-\frac18)=\frac79.

The direction perpendicular to AC on the outside is, as shown in the figure, (1,1)/sqrt(2), so let s=t/sqrt(2)=1/(2sqrt(2)), then D=(s,1+s). Starting from A, AB=(-1,0), AD=(s-1,1+s). Also |AD|=sqrt((s-1)^2+(1+s)^2)=3/2. Let θ=angle BAD, then cos θ=(1-s)/(3/2), sin θ=(1+s)/(3/2). Therefore sin(2θ)=2sinθcosθ=2*((1+s)/(3/2))*((1-s)/(3/2))=(8/9)(1-s^2). Since s^2=1/8, sin(2 angle BAD)=(8/9)(7/8)=7/9.
